subject: Chemistry
title: One Drop, Blood Red: Why Transition Metals Form Complexes
summary: A complex is a central metal ion bonded to several ligands (anions or neutral molecules) by coordinate bonds, in which the ligand gives both electrons. One drop of KSCN turns pale-yellow Fe³⁺ blood red as [Fe(SCN)(H₂O)₅]²⁺ forms, while the K⁺ from the same drop grabs nothing. Transition-metal ions form far more complexes because they are small (Fe³⁺ 65 pm vs K⁺ 138 pm), highly charged (+3 vs +1) and have d orbitals available for bond formation.

notes.title: 11 – Formation of Complex Compounds: Why Transition Metals Form Complexes

keyPoints: **Complex** = central metal ion + **ligands** (anions or neutral molecules) joined by coordinate bonds.
In a **coordinate bond** the ligand donates its **lone pair**: both electrons come from the ligand (L → M).
Transition-metal ions are **small** (Fe³⁺ 65 pm vs K⁺ 138 pm) and **highly charged** (+3 vs +1): they grip a lone pair strongly.
They also have **d orbitals available for bond formation**, so they form far more complexes (NCERT 4.3.11).

blocks.p: Shannon effective ionic radii, six-coordinate. Small and highly charged = strong attraction for a ligand's lone pair.
[Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ + SCN⁻ → [Fe(SCN)(H₂O)₅]²⁺ (blood red) + H₂O. One SCN⁻ replaces one water; the N atom donates its lone pair to Fe³⁺. K⁺ from KSCN stays a spectator.
